summary: Defines a mobility extension for the Host Identity Protocol, using a LOCATOR_SET parameter so a host can tell peers its alternate addresses. This keeps communication going when an IP address changes.

plainLanguage.summary: When you move house, you send friends your new address so letters still reach you. This lets a computer do that without losing its conversations.

questions: how does hip handle ip address changes
what is the hip locator_set parameter
what is credit based authorization in hip
subtitle: How a Host Identity Protocol host tells its peers about a new IP address without dropping the conversation.

tldr.problem: When a host's IP address changes, connections tied to that address break. HIP already separates a host's identity from its IP address, but the peer still has to learn where the host can now be reached, and must not be fooled into sending traffic somewhere else.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile host sends a HIP UPDATE packet carrying a LOCATOR_SET parameter (plus an ESP_INFO parameter) that lists its new address. The peer verifies the address with a nonce challenge, and may send a limited amount of data to it in the meantime under credit-based authorization.
tldr.outcome: Communication survives an address change on one or both hosts, with defences against redirection-based flooding. This RFC obsoletes RFC 5206 and moves multihoming procedures to RFC 8047.

today: RFC 8046 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2017. It obsoletes RFC 5206, and multihoming is specified separately in RFC 8047. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP, RFC 7401) uses public/private key pairs, not IP addresses, as host identities. Transport sockets and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) Security Associations are bound to those identities, and IP addresses are used only for packet forwarding. This separation makes mobility and multihoming possible.

This RFC defines a LOCATOR_SET parameter that lets a host tell a peer about alternate addresses where it can be reached, and the message flows needed for basic end-host mobility, including address verification. It also specifies how a HIP rendezvous server (RVS, RFC 8004) can help when both hosts move at once.

Out of scope are multihoming procedures (see RFC 8047), transports other than ESP, localized mobility management, and how transport protocols should react to an address change.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer has a name that never changes and an address that can. This document explains how to say 'my address changed, send mail here now' safely.

sections.title: Locators and the Operating Environment
sections.content:
HIP is a key establishment and parameter negotiation protocol. In a HIP stack, upper-layer protocols are bound to Host Identity Tags (HITs), not IP addresses, and the HIP sublayer maintains the binding between HITs and IP addresses. The ESP Security Parameter Index (SPI) associates an incoming packet with the right HITs. A function labelled MH in the RFC's architecture figure manages these bindings for mobility and for multihoming.

The RFC generalizes an address into a locator. A locator names a point of attachment to the network but may also carry extra demultiplexing context, such as an ESP SPI, transport ports or an IPv6 Flow Label. The extra context matters because, for example, certain IP addresses may need to be associated with certain SPIs to avoid violating the ESP anti-replay window.

A host can receive packets protected by a HIP-created ESP SA from any address, so it can change its address and keep sending without necessarily rekeying. Its peers, however, cannot send to the new address until they have reliably and securely updated the addresses they associate with the host.
sections.plainLanguage: Your name tag stays the same wherever you go. A locator is the name tag plus a note saying which door to knock on and which mailbox slot to use.

sections.title: How a Readdress Works
sections.content:
In the simplest case the mobile host has one interface, one address and one pair of SAs. On getting a new address (a break-before-make or a make-before-break change, either is fine) it sends an UPDATE carrying one LOCATOR_SET and one ESP_INFO parameter, plus a SEQ parameter so the packet is retransmitted until acknowledged. With no rekeying, the OLD SPI and NEW SPI in ESP_INFO are both the existing incoming SPI.

The peer validates the UPDATE and MUST verify the new address by putting a nonce in an ECHO_REQUEST parameter of its reply. It MAY start using the new address at once but MUST limit how much data it sends there until verification completes. The mobile host echoes the nonce in an ECHO_RESPONSE; on receipt, the peer treats the address as verified.

The mobile host may also rekey at the same time, by setting a new SPI and KEYMAT Index in ESP_INFO and optionally adding a DIFFIE_HELLMAN parameter. Verification can also be implicit: in some cases the arrival of data on a newly advertised SA may be enough.

If both hosts move at nearly the same time (the 'double-jump' problem), each side's UPDATE goes to a stale address. The RFC lets a host resend its UPDATE to the peer's rendezvous server, which rewrites the packet and adds FROM and RVS_HMAC parameters before forwarding it.

The RFC notes that IPv6 networks are expected to be renumbered more often than most IPv4 networks, and that renumbering looks like mobility to an end host, so the same procedures apply.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell your friend your new address. Your friend sends a secret word to that address, and you shout it back. That proves you really live there, and then the mail flows freely.

sections.title: The LOCATOR_SET Parameter
sections.content:
The LOCATOR_SET parameter has Type 193 and is a critical parameter, so a recipient MUST recognize and process it. It holds the usual HIP Type and Length fields plus zero or more Locator sub-parameters. Each one carries a Traffic Type, Locator Type, Locator Length, a Reserved field, a preferred-locator P bit, a Locator Lifetime and the Locator itself. An empty LOCATOR_SET is allowed and deprecates all addresses.

Traffic Type is 0 for both signaling and user data, 1 for HIP signaling only and 2 for data only. The P bit marks the locator as preferred for that traffic type, and the more specific type wins on conflict. Locator Type 0 is a 128-bit IPv6 address (or IPv4-in-IPv6 format address). Type 1 is a 32-bit ESP SPI followed by such an address.

Every locator MUST have a non-zero lifetime in seconds. When it passes, the address is expected to become deprecated, and a deprecated address SHOULD NOT be used as a destination if a non-deprecated one with sufficient scope is available. An UPDATE with a LOCATOR_SET SHOULD include both an HMAC and a HIP_SIGNATURE parameter, and MAY include a HOST_ID parameter, which the receiver MUST then check against the one used to set up the association.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of addresses where you can be found. Each entry says how long it is good for and whether it is your favorite.

sections.title: Locator States and Processing Rules
sections.content:
Each locator is tracked with its bit pattern, lifetime, traffic type scope, preferred flag and a status: UNVERIFIED (reachability not yet checked), ACTIVE (verified and not deprecated) or DEPRECATED (lifetime expired). A deprecated address MUST NOT become active without first verifying its reachability. The addresses used in the base exchange start as preferred, ACTIVE, with an unbounded lifetime.

A host sends a LOCATOR_SET whenever it sees a change to its addresses on an active association that will last at least a few seconds, and SHOULD avoid rapid changes. A new LOCATOR_SET replaces the earlier one, so it must list all active locators. Hosts MUST NOT announce broadcast or multicast addresses.

A receiver processes ESP_INFO first, deciding from the OLD and NEW SPI whether this is a no-op, a rekey, a new SA or a deprecation. It then checks each locator, adds or refreshes it as UNVERIFIED, and marks listed-nowhere addresses on that SPI as DEPRECATED. It MUST detect and skip a duplicate LOCATOR_SET that arrives via several paths. Unsupported locator types may trigger a LOCATOR_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED NOTIFY error.

Switching to a new preferred locator requires first verifying its address. Meanwhile the host SHOULD use another ACTIVE locator if one exists, or MAY use the new one as far as credit-based authorization allows.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address in your list is marked 'not checked yet', 'checked and good' or 'too old'. You only trust the good ones, and old ones must be checked again.

sections.title: Credit-Based Authorization
sections.content:
Waiting for address verification can slow applications, so the RFC defines credit-based authorization (CBA). Its idea is that a flooding attacker wants to amplify traffic, so CBA limits what a host sends to an unverified address to the amount of data recently received from that peer.

A host keeps a credit counter per peer. Each arriving packet raises the counter by its size. A packet to an UNVERIFIED preferred locator is sent only if no ACTIVE locator exists and the counter is higher than the packet size; sending reduces the counter by the packet size. Otherwise the packet MUST be discarded or buffered until verification succeeds. Sending to an ACTIVE locator does not change the counter.

To stop an attacker building credit slowly and spending it in one burst, counters are aged: multiplied by CreditAgingFactor every CreditAgingInterval. The RFC proposes 7/8 and 5 seconds, which work for a TCP file transfer when the round-trip time does not exceed 500 milliseconds. How to set the credit limit is not specified, but a heuristic is enough credit to keep the sending rate for two or three round-trip times.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you may only lend a stranger as many sweets as they gave you first. A trickster cannot get a huge pile from you for free, and the credit slowly shrinks so they cannot save it up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because HIP verifies the sender of an UPDATE cryptographically (HMAC and signature), forging or replaying one is very difficult. The RFC therefore focuses on two threats: malicious redirection of legitimate connections and redirection-based flooding.

For impersonation, the base exchange authentication and UPDATE signatures prevent an attacker from redirecting a connection, and ownership of an association is tied to a HIP identity, so the real owner can reclaim a hijacked connection. A man-in-the-middle can only act if present at the base exchange and the hosts do not authenticate each other.

For flooding, an attacker could start a large download and redirect it to a victim. Reachability checks and CBA do not eliminate flooding but rule out use from off the path to the victim and any amplification, lowering it to the level of a direct flood. Against memory exhaustion, an association SHOULD limit the number of IP addresses tied to any one identity. The RFC also discusses mixed HIP and non-HIP environments, and privacy: implementations SHOULD let an administrator block exposure of selected addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the real owner can say 'I moved', because the message is signed. And no one can trick a computer into blasting a stranger with a huge flood of data.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 5206
sections.content:
This RFC extends HIP Version 2, while RFC 5206 extended Version 1. RFC 5206 covered both mobility and basic multihoming. Here only mobility remains, and multihoming is specified in RFC 8047.

Other changes: the LOCATOR parameter is renamed LOCATOR_SET; text was added for double-jump and make-before-break mobility; a host may add the source address of a received HIP packet as a candidate locator while preferring listed ones; the HOST_ID parameter is allowed in UPDATEs; only a single LOCATOR_SET and ESP_INFO in an UPDATE is specified; a simple heuristic for CBA credit is given; and hosts MUST avoid reprocessing redundant LOCATOR_SETs.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the newer edition of the rulebook. It does just the moving-house part and leaves the many-addresses part to a sister document.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets, excluding Type, Length and padding.

fields.name: Locator Length
fields.desc: Length of the Locator in 4-byte words.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero when sent, ignored when received.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Set to one if the locator is preferred for that Traffic Type.

fields.name: Locator Lifetime
fields.desc: How long the locator is expected to be valid, in seconds.

fields.name: Locator
fields.desc: The locator; the sub-parameter from Traffic Type onward repeats for each locator.
